outcomes.text: 5. What makes a new person feel welcome?

explainers.title: Read this with your grown-up
explainers.body:
Amara goes to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. This year a new girl called Imani joined her class. Imani had just moved from far away, so everything felt new and a little bit scary. On the first morning, Amara walked over and said hello. She learned to say Imani's name, and asked her to sit together. At playtime, she asked Imani to join the game. Soon Imani was smiling. One kind hello made all the difference! In these activities, you will get ready to welcome a new friend, just like Amara did.

After a few days, Imani felt brave enough to share something from home. She taught the class a song her family loved. Everyone joined in, even though the words were new. When we welcome someone, we get a lovely gift back too — we learn about their world.

explainers.title: 1. My family
explainers.body:
Draw a picture of your family in the box below. Draw the people who love and care for you. If you know where your family comes from, you can draw that too — the sea, a city, a town, or a faraway place.

My family comes from ____________________________________________.

explainers.title: 2. Meet some friends
explainers.body:
Read about three friends who live in different places. Leila lives in a big, busy city with tall buildings and markets. Ben lives in a small town by the sea, where the boats come in every evening. Far away, Rohan lives in a city where it snows in winter! Their homes look very different — but all three have families, all three say hello to their friends, and all three love to play.

Now draw your own home, and one thing you love about it.

One thing that is the same for me, Leila, Ben and Rohan is ____________________.

explainers.title: 3. A treasure from home
explainers.body:
A heritage treasure is a special thing your family shares. It could be a food you love, a song you sing, a game you play, or a word your family says. For example, Amara's treasure is her grandmother's story about the fishing boats in Berbera. What is yours? Draw or write one treasure here.

My treasure is ________________________________________________.

explainers.title: 4. Saying hello
explainers.body:
In our class, we say hello. All around the world, people say hello in lots of lovely ways. Ask your family how they say hello at home, and write it here. Then teach it to a friend!

Here are some kind words you can use when you meet someone new. Read them out loud with your grown-up:
bullets: Hello! I am glad you are here.
Would you like to play with me?

headers: At home, we say hello like this:

explainers.title: 5. What makes a new person feel welcome?
explainers.body:
Imagine a new child has just joined your class. Read each kind thing below. Tick the box next to the ones you could do to help them feel welcome.

Now draw one more kind idea of your very own:

rows: Learn their name and say it kindly.
Ask them to play with you.
Give them a big, friendly smile.

explainers.title: 6. How would you feel?
explainers.body:
Imagine you are the new child. It is your first day. You do not know anyone yet. Circle the words that show how you might feel: happy, shy, worried, excited, lonely, curious. A new day can feel like lots of things at once, and that is okay.

Now think what would help you feel better. Write one kind thing you would want a classmate to do for you.

headers: On my first day, I might feel ...
It would help me if someone ...

explainers.title: 7. A warm hello
explainers.body:
In this box, draw yourself saying hello to a new classmate, just like Amara did for Imani. Give both of you a big happy face!

One kind thing I could say is: __________________________________.

explainers.title: 8. Think and share
explainers.body:
Talk about these questions with your grown-up. You can draw or write your answers on the lines.

Well done! You are ready to be a wonderful welcomer. Keep these activities safe — you will use all of your kind ideas in the final project, when your team makes a real welcome for a new friend.

headers: How do you think a newcomer might feel on their very first day?
What is one great thing about living where you live?
Where near your home would you like to show a new friend? Why?
What kind thing will you do for the next new person you meet?

bigIdeas.title: A little help from your grown-up
lines: Grown-ups can hold the camera or help with spelling.
Keep it short and cheerful — about one minute of video, or one bright poster.
The most important thing is the kindness, not being perfect.

bigIdeas.title: Give yourself a star
lines: You thought about how someone else feels.
You made something kind to help them belong.
That is what a good friend does. Well done!

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With a grown-up, tell your AI tutor about the welcome you made.
Ask it: what is one more kind thing that would make a newcomer smile?
Practise saying your welcome words out loud together.

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.

sections.title: About this unit
sections.body:
Welcome to the last unit of Year 3 Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This unit is called You are welcome! It is a warm, gentle unit about where our families come from, the special things families pass on, and how we can make a new person feel happy and safe when they join us.

Global Perspectives is a little different from other subjects. It is not about learning lots of facts by heart. It is about growing helpful thinking and caring skills through a real topic. In this unit the topic is family, heritage and welcoming newcomers, and the skills are all about understanding our own story, listening to other people, and being kind.

This is a lovely topic for children in the Horn of Africa. Many of our families have wonderful stories of movement and heritage. Grandparents may have grown up by the sea in Berbera, in a busy city like Mogadishu, or in a small village far from town. Some children have family who came from another country. Every one of these stories is interesting and worth being proud of.

This guide is written for you, the grown-up — the teacher or the parent leading the way. The children are only seven or eight, so you will read, talk and do the activities together. Everything is kept short, simple and picture-led.

The unit builds slowly towards one happy project. After six little lessons, the children make a real welcome for a child who is new to their class — a friendly video, or a bright poster or booklet. So as you go, you are always heading somewhere kind: every lesson adds one more idea about how to make a newcomer feel they belong.

sections.title: The skills your child will grow
sections.body:
Three big Global Perspectives skills grow in this unit. You do not need to name them for the children — just help them practise:

Along the way children also do a little gentle research (asking family, looking at pictures) and a little working together (making something as a team). But the heart of the unit is kindness and understanding.

Welcoming is a real skill, and it is one of the kindest a child can learn. A newcomer who is met with a warm hello, a learned name and an invitation to play will remember it for years. When children practise this now, they are learning to notice how another person feels and to do something kind about it. That gift stays with them well beyond this unit.
items: Reflecting on our own story. Children think about their own family and where it comes from, and begin to feel proud and curious about it.
Listening to others. Children learn to listen kindly when a friend or a family member shares their story, and to ask gentle questions.
Welcoming. Children imagine how a new person feels and choose kind actions that help someone feel they belong.

sections.title: How this unit works
sections.body:
At Ehel Academy, young learners are led by a grown-up. Three kinds of help work together in this unit:

You will also see Ask Your Family boxes. These invite the child to talk to someone at home about the family's story. This is one of the warmest parts of the unit, so give it time and treat every answer as a treasure.

Keep every sitting playful. Chat more than you write, use lots of pictures, and let the child use their home language whenever it helps. If a child wants to teach you a word from home, that is a wonderful moment — celebrate it. The mood you are aiming for is warm, curious and gentle, never a test.
items: You, the grown-up. You read each little lesson with the child, talk about the questions, and help with the drawing and making. You are the guide.
Your teacher sessions, about twice a week. In these live sessions children share their work, practise welcoming each other, and learn from their classmates.

Your AI tutor, used together with a grown-up. A few times in this unit you will see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box. Here a grown-up helps the child talk to the AI tutor, to hear a friendly example, get an idea, or practise saying kind words. The grown-up always stays with the child for these moments.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: Introduce these words gently, in your own speech, as they come up. There is no need for the children to write definitions.

rows: The people who love and care for you. Families come in many shapes and sizes.
The special things a family passes on, such as stories, food, language and songs.
When living things move to a new place. Some animals migrate every year.
To make someone feel happy, safe and glad to be here.
Someone who has just arrived somewhere new.

sections.title: What you will need
items: Paper, pencils and colouring pens.
The Activity Sheet (File 2) and the Mini-Project and Reflection sheet (File 3).
A device with the AI tutor, used together with a grown-up.
A phone or tablet that can film — only if you choose to make a welcome video (this is optional).
Optional: a family photo, or a small object from home, that the child would like to share — only if they want to.

sections.title: A note on care and kindness
sections.body: This unit touches families, heritage and moving to new places. These can be tender subjects for some children, so please hold them with care. A few gentle rules keep this unit warm and safe for everyone:
items: Keep it positive and never political. When we talk about people moving, keep the reasons simple and kind — to be near family, for a new job, to go to school, or to find a happy, safe home.
Let children share only what they want to. Never press a child to talk about their family. A drawing, a single word, or nothing at all is completely fine.
Celebrate every family. A family that has always lived in one town has a story just as special as a family that has travelled far. No story is better than another.
Be even-handed and fair. Children come from different backgrounds and celebrate different special days. Welcome all of them equally and kindly.
Watch for tender moments. If a story brings up a big feeling, pause, be gentle, and move on to something warm. It is always fine to say that some things are private.

sections.title: Meet Amara
sections.body:
To make the unit friendly, we follow one Year 3 child all the way through. Her name is Amara, and she is a learner at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. Amara loves stories, especially the ones her grandmother tells about growing up near the sea.

This year a new girl has joined Amara's class. Her name is Imani. Imani and her family have just moved to Hargeisa from another country, so everything is new to her — the school, the streets, and all the faces. Amara remembers her own first day and decides she will help Imani feel welcome. As you go through the unit, you will see little moments from Amara and Imani's story.

sections.title: The six little lessons
sections.body: Each little lesson has the same three simple parts: an Aim (what it is for), Talk about (gentle questions to chat about together), and Do (a small thing to make or try). Read them with the child and take your time.

sections.title: Lesson 1: Where do our families come from?
sections.body: Aim. Children notice that every family has a story about where it comes from, and that these stories are interesting and worth sharing.

sections.title: Talk about.
sections.body: Do. The child draws a simple picture of their family on the Activity Sheet, and, if they know, where the family comes from. They tell you one thing they found out.
items: Does everyone in our class come from exactly the same place?
Where were your grandparents born? Do you know?
What could we learn from a friend whose family comes from somewhere else?

sections.title: Lesson 2: What is migration?
sections.body: Aim. Children meet the word migration in a gentle way, starting with animals, and learn that moving to a new place is a natural part of life.

sections.title: Talk about.
sections.body:
Do. Look together at an animal that migrates. Good examples are birds that fly to warmer places when it gets cold and come back later, or the great herds of wildebeest that move across the plains of East Africa following the rain and the fresh grass. Talk about why they move, and that they often return.

Then, very gently, connect it to people: people sometimes move to new places too. They might move to be near family, for a new job, to go to school, or to find a happy and safe home. Moving somewhere new can feel exciting and a little bit scary at the same time.
items: Do you know any animals that travel a very long way?
Why might an animal move to a new place? (To find food, warmer weather, or a safe place.)
Do the animals come back again?

sections.title: Lesson 3: What is different, and the same, about our places?
sections.body: Aim. Children notice that places around the world can look different, but that people everywhere need similar things — a home, food, family, friends and kindness.

sections.title: Talk about.
sections.body: Do. Meet three friends who live in different places. Leila lives in a busy city with tall buildings and markets that seem never to sleep. Ben lives in a small town by the sea, where the fishing boats come in every evening. Far away, Rohan lives in a city where it turns cold and snowy in winter. Their homes look very different — but all three have families, all three say hello to their friends, and all three love to play. Then the child draws their own home and one thing they love about it.
items: What does our town look like? What can you see, hear and smell here?
What might a big, busy city look like? What about a small town by the sea?
What do all these places have that is the same?

sections.title: Lesson 4: What is your family heritage?
sections.body: Aim. Children explore their own heritage — the special foods, words, songs and stories a family passes on — and practise listening kindly when someone shares theirs.

sections.title: Talk about.
sections.body:
Do. If you can, invite a family member to visit and talk about where the family comes from. Or simply ask at home. Help the child practise listening in a kind, polite way, using friendly phrases such as: That is so interesting! Can you tell me more? Sorry, could you say that again please? The child draws or writes one heritage treasure on the Activity Sheet.

Families enjoy different special days, and all of them are lovely. Some families look forward most to Eid. Some love Christmas. Some treasure a harvest day, or a naming day for a new baby. Every one of these is special to the family who shares it, and it is kind to be curious about them all.
items: What is heritage? (The special things our family passes on to us.)
What special food does your family love to cook?
Is there a song, a word, or a story your family shares?

sections.title: Lesson 5: What is it like starting at a new school?
sections.body: Aim. Children imagine how a newcomer feels and think of kind, real actions to help someone feel welcome. This is the heart of the whole unit.

sections.title: Talk about.
sections.body: Do. Together make a list of kind actions that help a newcomer. Then act it out: one child pretends to be new, and the others practise welcoming them — saying hello, learning their name, showing them around, and asking them to play. Keep it gentle and full of smiles.
items: Imagine it is your very first day at a brand-new school. What might feel hard?
Maybe not knowing where things are, not knowing anyone, or speaking a new language.
How would you like other children to treat you on that day?

sections.title: Lesson 6: What is great about living here?
sections.body: Aim. Children feel proud of where they live and get ready to share it warmly with a new friend.

sections.title: Talk about.
sections.body: Do. In a small group, make a bright poster of good things about living here. Give everyone a job so it feels fair: a leader, one or two writers, one or two drawers, and a helper who fetches the materials. Good poster tips: a big clear title, lots of pictures, only a few short words, and cheerful colours. This poster is a lovely warm-up for the final task.
items: What do you love about where you live?
Is it the food, the people, a special place, or something you like to do?
What would you most want a new friend to know about our home?

sections.title: The Final Task: a welcome for a new classmate
sections.body:
The unit finishes with a kind, joyful project. In a small team, the children make a welcome for a child who is new to their class — just like Amara welcoming Imani. There are two ways to do it, so pick whichever suits your group:

The full child-friendly, step-by-step plan is in File 3, the Mini-Project and Reflection sheet. Children do it with a grown-up close by. The aim is simple: to make a real newcomer feel happy, safe and glad to be here.

Everything from the earlier lessons feeds in here. The children already know how a newcomer might feel, they have practised kind hellos, and they have thought about what is great about their home. Now they simply put it together into one warm welcome. Encourage them to use their own words, and remind them that a short, honest, kind message is far better than a long or fancy one.
items: A welcome video — the team says warm hello words to the camera and shows the new friend around.
A welcome poster or booklet — the team draws and writes a friendly guide to the class and school.

sections.title: Thinking back together
sections.body:
At the end, sit with the child and think back over the unit. Keep it light and kind. The reflection sheet in File 3 has simple prompts, but you can also just chat about these:

That is the whole unit. If the children finish it a little kinder, a little prouder of their own story, and a little quicker to welcome a new friend, then You are welcome! has done its job beautifully. Thank you for guiding them.
items: What did you enjoy most in this unit?
What are you proud of?
What is one kind thing you did to help someone feel welcome?
How did your team work together on the final task?

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro:
Make a welcome for a new classmate

This is your big project for the unit. You will make a warm welcome for a child who is new to your class — just like Amara welcomed Imani. Do it with your team and a grown-up close by. It will be kind, and it will be fun!

A welcome is a kind way of saying: I am happy you are here, and you belong with us. When someone is new, a welcome helps them feel safe instead of scared. In this project, you and your team will make a welcome that a real new classmate could see one day.

steps.title: How might they feel?
steps.intro: Close your eyes and imagine it is your first day at a brand-new school. Talk about how a newcomer might feel. They might feel shy, or a bit worried, and maybe excited too. When you remember that feeling, it helps you know exactly what would make them feel better.

rows: We talked about how a new child might feel.

steps.title: Plan what to show
steps.intro: Decide what would help a new friend most. You could show your classroom, the playground, where to line up, where to get a drink of water, and the kind faces in your class. Pick the things that would make a newcomer feel safe and happy. Write or draw your plan in the box.

headers: Our plan — what we will show

steps.title: Write your welcome words
steps.intro:
Now write a few warm words to say. You do not need many — kind and simple is best. Here are some sentence starters to help you:

Try to use kind, happy words, like: welcome, glad, friend, happy, safe, together, smile. Say your words out loud first — if they sound warm and friendly, they are just right.
items: Hello and welcome to our class at Ehel Academy!
My name is ____ and I am so glad you are here.
Let me show you ____.
One great thing about our school is ____.
If you need a friend, you can come to me.
We are really happy you joined us!

steps.title: Make it
steps.intro:
Now make your welcome! Give everyone in the team a job so it feels fair, and take turns.

Use bright colours and big, clear letters, so your welcome is easy and happy to look at. Remember, it does not have to be perfect — it just has to be kind.
items: If you chose a video: practise your words, then film them with a grown-up. Smile at the camera!
If you chose a poster or booklet: draw the pictures, write the big title, and add your warm words.

steps.title: Share your welcome
steps.intro: Show your welcome to your class or your family. Stand up tall, look at the person, and say your words warmly, with a big smile. If you made a video, play it for everyone. If you made a poster, hold it up and read it out. You have made someone feel they belong — that is a wonderful thing to do.

steps.title: Before you go
steps.intro:
You have finished your welcome — what a kind thing to make! Chat about these last questions with your team or your grown-up. Remember, there are no wrong answers.

You did it! In this unit you have learned about families, heritage and welcoming newcomers. Best of all, you have made a real welcome that could help someone feel they belong. That is the kindest kind of clever. Well done — you are welcome!
items: What did you enjoy most about making your welcome?
What are you most proud of?
What was a little bit tricky, and how did you sort it out?
How did your team work together?
What is one kind thing you will keep doing for new friends?

reflection.prompt: This part is called reflection. It just means thinking back about how we did, so we can feel proud and get even better next time. Tick Yes or Getting there for each one. Be kind to yourself — every try counts!

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: Our welcome helps a new child feel happy and safe.
Our welcome shows the kind things about our class.
Everyone in our team helped in some way.
We shared the jobs and worked together.
I said or did something kind for a newcomer.
